structure.title: I.
structure.summary: On a cold, wet night at Laburnam Villa, Mr. White and his son Herbert play chess while Mrs. White knits by a fire; their isolation and strained family dynamics are evident as Mr. White vents frustration about their remote location. Sergeant-Major Morris arrives by foot after a long journey, bringing with him a dried monkey’s paw said to grant three wishes to three men, each cursed by tragic consequences. He recounts how the first owner used his third wish for death, warning the family against using it, yet Mr. White, despite the soldier’s urgent pleas to burn it, retrieves the paw from the fire and keeps it. After supper, Herbert jests about wishing for wealth, prompting Mr. White to reluctantly wish for two hundred pounds, after which the paw twists violently in his hand—causing shock and unease—and the family is left unsettled as the wind howls outside.

structure.title: II.
structure.summary: The chapter opens on a bright winter morning at the White family home, where the father, Mr. White, dismisses his previous night's fears about the monkey's paw, treating it as a foolish superstition. The family shares a lighthearted breakfast, with Herbert joking about the paw's power and Mrs. White mocking her husband’s credulity. Later, during dinner, Mr. White insists the paw moved in his hand, prompting his wife to notice a well-dressed stranger hesitating outside their house. The man enters, visibly uneasy, and identifies himself as a representative from 'Maw and Meggins.' He delivers the devastating news that Herbert has been killed in a machinery accident at work, and though the company disclaims liability, they offer two hundred pounds as compensation. Upon hearing the exact sum, Mr. White collapses unconscious, overcome by the horrifying confirmation of the paw’s supernatural power.

structure.title: III.
structure.summary: In the quiet, shadowed house two miles from the cemetery, the elderly couple grieves silently after the death of their son, Herbert, until the wife, overcome by grief, remembers the monkey’s paw and demands her husband use it to wish their son back to life. Despite his terror and warnings about the mutilated state of the body, the husband reluctantly retrieves the paw from the parlour mantelpiece and makes the second wish. The house falls into oppressive silence until a stealthy knock sounds at the front door — repeated, growing louder — and the wife, convinced it is Herbert, rushes to open it. The husband, in panic, searches the floor for the paw and makes a final, desperate third wish just as the bolt is drawn back, silencing the knocks. The street outside is empty and deserted when he reaches the gate.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
On a cold, wet night at the isolated Laburnam Villa, Mr. White, his wife Mrs. White, and their son Herbert share a tense, quiet evening marked by emotional distance and unspoken frustrations. Their solitude is shattered by the arrival of Sergeant-Major Morris, a weary traveler who brings with him a dried monkey’s paw rumored to grant three wishes—each cursed by devastating consequences. Though Morris urgently warns them to destroy it, Mr. White, intrigued and defiant, retrieves the paw from the fire. In a moment of dark humor, Herbert jokes about wishing for money, prompting Mr. White to reluctantly wish for two hundred pounds; the paw twists violently in his hand, leaving the family shaken but dismissive as the wind howls outside.

The next morning, the Whites try to laugh off the night’s events, treating the paw as a superstition, until the grim reality of their wish unfolds. A somber representative from Maw and Meggins arrives to inform them that Herbert has died in a machinery accident—and the company offers exactly two hundred pounds in compensation. The chilling coincidence shatters Mr. White’s skepticism and collapses him into unconsciousness, revealing the paw’s terrifying power. Grief overtakes the household, isolating the couple in their sorrow as they retreat from the world, haunted by the echo of their son’s laughter and the weight of their careless wish.

Driven by unbearable grief, Mrs. White insists her husband use the paw to bring Herbert back to life. Terrified but powerless against her anguish, Mr. White makes the second wish—and the house is plunged into an unnatural silence, broken only by a slow, deliberate knock at the front door. As Mrs. White rushes to open it, convinced it is her son, Mr. White realizes the horror of what they’ve summoned: a mangled, unnatural version of Herbert. In a final act of desperate love, he scrambles for the paw and makes his third wish just as the bolt is drawn back. When he stumbles outside, the street is empty—no trace of the knock, no sign of his son, only the chilling stillness of a world that has been forever altered by their meddling with forces beyond comprehension.
